notes.h: Effect of developing technology on industry (Higher Level only)
notes.b: New technology changes how work is organised, how many workers are needed and which skills are in demand. Some effects are gains for workers and some are losses, and exam answers need both.
points: Automation (machines and robots taking over repetitive production and processing tasks) means fewer workers are needed for the same output, because the machines do the routine work.
Increased output with fewer workers reduces working hours in some industries, which gives people more leisure time, but it also removes jobs at the lower-skilled end.

Computers and electronic communication change office work. They create new skilled jobs to design, install, maintain and operate the technology, so jobs shift towards programming, supervising and maintaining.

Electronic communication allows home working (teleworking), which suits some people. The downside is that it makes it harder to switch off from work, and it reduces face-to-face social contact at work.
Technology also makes work safer and cleaner in some settings, because dangerous and dirty tasks are carried out by machines. This means fewer injuries and healthier workplaces.
Workers whose skills become out of date, or who lose unskilled and manual jobs, need retraining. Companies can also relocate production to low-cost countries, which removes jobs at home.
Technology has also changed office and service work: banking, shopping and booking online mean fewer counter and clerical jobs and more technical ones.
notes.tip: Analyse questions ask for positive and negative effects, so give at least two of each (for example safer work and new skilled jobs against loss of manual jobs and difficulty switching off), and explain each one.

notes.h: Decline of primary and secondary industry and growth of services (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Employment has moved from extracting and manufacturing towards services. To describe the shift you first need to know the three kinds of industry.
points: Primary industry extracts resources from the land and sea: agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining or quarrying (such as peat).
Secondary industry manufactures and processes primary raw materials into finished goods, for example food processing, clothing, engineering and construction.

Tertiary (service) industry provides services such as tourism, leisure, healthcare, transport, media, retail, education, banking and finance, hospitality and IT. Note that tertiary means services, not third-level education.

Automation and mechanisation reduced the number of manufacturing and farming jobs because machines do more of the work. Service industries expanded and absorbed many workers as incomes rose and demand for services grew.
Companies relocated production to lower-cost countries, causing job losses in manufacturing in Ireland. Growth of tourism, finance and technology firms added service jobs.

The effects on people were that manual and unskilled workers were displaced and rural areas lost jobs, while urban areas gained service jobs. Service work brought more part-time and shift work and a new demand for qualified workers.

Setting: compare Ireland's current occupational structure with that of fifty years ago, noting the shift from farming, factory and other manual work to service and professional work. Describe the pattern without figures.
notes.tip: Remember the shift is about where people work, not that farming or manufacturing has stopped: both still exist and produce more with fewer workers. Don't write 'tertiary' as meaning third-level education.

notes.b: As jobs have shifted towards services and technology, employers increasingly expect higher qualifications. Education has become the way into work and the way to move up within it.
points: Service and technology jobs need literacy, numeracy, computing and communication skills, which are developed through education.

Employers use qualifications to select between applicants, so a larger share of applicants now hold them. The Leaving Certificate is the minimum for many jobs, and many need a further education or higher qualification.
Qualifications widen employment options and allow career advancement, because they show an employer what a worker can do.
Early school leavers and unskilled workers find it difficult to acquire work, as many jobs require a minimum level of education. They are most at risk of unemployment and low pay.
Continuing education, such as evening courses, distance learning and part-time courses, allows adults to gain qualifications, keep pace with technology, improve promotion prospects or change career.
Upskilling programmes (courses that build on skills a worker already has) also let adults keep their skills up to date.
Reskilling (training in new skills) allows workers whose jobs have disappeared to move into new occupations.
notes.tip: Questions on education and employment look for these points: qualifications widen options, early leavers struggle, reskilling helps displaced workers, and the Leaving Certificate is the minimum for many jobs.

notes.h: Increased participation by women (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Many more women, including married women and mothers, are now in paid work than in the middle of the twentieth century. The causes are social and economic, and each one needs a short reason.
points: Women are better educated than in the past, and qualifications open access to professional and skilled work.
Equality legislation removed barriers: the Civil Service (Employment of Married Women) Act 1973 removed the marriage bar (the rule forcing married women to leave civil service jobs).
The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 first legislated for equal pay for equal work. Both Acts are now covered by the Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015.
Income from paid work gives women financial independence, self-esteem, status and a stronger personal identity, as well as social contact outside the home.
The growth of service industries and part-time work created many jobs that suited women's skills and flexible hours.
Rising living, housing and child care costs, and the need for a second income, encourage women into paid employment. More marital breakdown and lone parenthood also make earning necessary.
Flexible hours, job-sharing, term-time work, maternity and parental leave and career breaks make it possible to combine paid work with home and family responsibilities.

More child care facilities, labour-saving appliances and smaller families free up women's time, and changing attitudes make work more accepted. The result is financial independence for women and more dual-earner families (both parents earning).
notes.tip: Examiners ask for three or four reasons, each explained, so pick distinct ones such as education, equal pay, cost of living and flexible work, and add a reason to each. Don't quote percentages of women in the workforce.

notes.b: Pay, safety and time off have all improved, which made paid work more attractive. These improvements also enabled women to take part in the workforce more fully.
points: Better pay, including the introduction of the minimum wage, plus pension entitlement and paid holiday arrangements, make paid work more attractive.
Statutory protections for workers (those set down in law) cover health and safety, pay and working time. Employment is protected by legislation, as are equal pay and equality law.
Safer and cleaner workplaces, made possible by technology, reduce risk of injury and illness. Working hours are also shorter than in the past.

Statutory leave includes maternity leave, parental leave and force majeure leave (urgent family reasons). Parental leave and career breaks let workers take time away for family reasons and return to their job.
Facilities for working parents, such as crèches and breastfeeding breaks, make it easier to stay in work after having a child.
Improved conditions have enabled many women to return to the workforce after raising children, because work no longer has to be given up for family life.
notes.tip: If asked how improved conditions enabled women to take part in work, link each improvement to women: flexible hours, parental and maternity leave, job-sharing, teleworking, career break, term-time work, crèches, equal pay and minimum wage.

notes.h: Increasing flexibility in working hours (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Working time is now arranged in many ways other than the traditional full-time, fixed-hours week. These arrangements let workers fit paid work around family life.
points: Flexitime: employees choose their start and finish times within agreed core hours, when everyone must be at work.
Job-sharing: two people share one full-time post, dividing the hours, pay and duties between them.
Part-time and term-time working: reduced hours, or work arranged around the school year, which suits parents of school-age children.
Compressed or reduced working weeks, such as working longer days across fewer days, and teleworking: working from home or another remote location using electronic communication.
Career breaks: an agreed period of unpaid leave, after which the worker returns to their job.

Parental leave: under the Parental Leave Act 1998 (as amended), parents are entitled to unpaid leave to look after a young child, currently 26 weeks per child for a child under 12 (longer if the child has a disability or long-term illness).
It is taken in one block or in agreed blocks, and it is not paid by the employer by right.

Related leaves exist under other laws: maternity leave (Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004), paternity leave (Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016), parent's leave (Parent's Leave and Benefit Act 2019), carer's leave (Carer's Leave Act 2001) and force majeure leave.
notes.tip: Teleworking and job-sharing are working arrangements, not types of leave, and parental leave is unpaid. For flexible working questions give examples with an explanation, plus one clear benefit and one drawback.

notes.h: Flexible and remote working requests (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The law now gives employees a right to ask for flexible hours or to work remotely. The employer does not have to agree, but must handle the request fairly.
points: The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 provides these rights, and the flexible and remote working provisions commenced on 6 March 2024.
Parents and carers of children up to 12 (or up to 16 if the child is disabled or long-term ill), and carers, can request flexible working. Any employee can request remote working.
The employer must consider the request and reply in writing within set time limits, giving reasons for any refusal, so workers get a clear answer.
The Act also provides paid domestic-violence leave (5 days, from November 2023) and unpaid medical care leave (from 3 July 2023).

notes.h: Effects of changing patterns of work (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Taken together, the changes in technology, industry, education, women's work and working hours affect individuals and families in both helpful and difficult ways.
points: Workers displaced from manufacturing may need retraining before they can find work in services, so the availability of work changes for individuals.
Flexible working helps parents plan childcare and family life more smoothly. It means more time with children, less stress and an easier balance of work and family.
Blurred boundaries between work and home can increase stress and make it harder to switch off.
Flexible working can also mean lower income, slower promotion, a shortfall in pension and resentment from colleagues.
Families in which both parents work gain income but may face role overload and role conflict, because family tasks still have to be done.
Employers gain access to a wider, more skilled labour pool and can keep staff by offering flexible arrangements.
notes.tip: For effects on individuals and families, give one individual effect (such as retraining or work-life balance) and one family effect (such as dual-earner households or the need for child care), then add others. Work-life balance answers need a benefit and a drawback.

keyTerms.definition: The use of machines or robots to carry out tasks previously done by people, reducing the number of workers needed.
Industry that extracts natural resources, such as agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining.
Industry that manufactures or processes primary raw materials into finished goods.
Industry that provides services, such as tourism, healthcare, transport, media and education.
The distribution of employment across types of occupation, such as manual, service and professional work.
A working arrangement in which employees choose their start and finish times within agreed core hours.
An arrangement in which two people share the hours and pay of one full-time post.
Working from home or another remote location, using electronic communication to stay connected with the employer.
Training workers in new skills so they can move into different occupations.
Unpaid leave that parents can take to care for a child, in one block or spread over an agreed period.

factCards.definition: Primary: extraction of resources such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. Secondary: manufacturing and processing of raw materials into goods. Tertiary: services such as tourism, healthcare, transport, media and education.
Flexitime, where workers choose start and finish times within core hours; job-sharing, where two people share one post; part-time or term-time working; teleworking from home or a remote location.

factCards.term: Three effects of developing technology on work
factCards.definition: Automation reduces the number of workers needed for repetitive tasks; new skilled jobs are created to design and maintain technology; electronic communication blurs the boundary between work and home.

factCards.term: Two reasons for increased educational requirements
factCards.definition: Service and technology jobs need higher skills, and employers use qualifications to select between a growing number of qualified applicants.

factCards.term: Four reasons for increased participation by women
factCards.definition: Better education; financial independence; flexible hours and part-time work; the need for a second income to meet living costs.

factCards.term: Two ways flexible hours help working parents
factCards.definition: They allow parents to plan childcare around work schedules; they let parents spend more time with children, such as through a reduced working week.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which the decline of primary and secondary industry has changed employment in Ireland.
questions.model: Manufacturing jobs were lost as automation reduced the number of workers needed, and some companies relocated production to lower-cost countries. Employment grew instead in tertiary (service) industries such as tourism, healthcare, transport and education.

questions.prompt: Analyse how the growth of service industries and the increased participation of women have together changed the structure of the workforce. Give examples of the working arrangements that have supported this change.
questions.model: Service industries grew as manufacturing and primary industries declined, creating many jobs in tourism, healthcare, retail, transport and education. These jobs often suited the skills and flexible hours that many women wanted, so women's participation rose. Women's participation was supported by better education, increased need for a second income, and improved working conditions. Working arrangements supporting this change include flexitime, job-sharing, part-time and term-time working, teleworking and parental leave. Increased participation changed the workforce by raising the number of families in which both parents work and increasing demand for childcare.
